title: What Are You Really After?
context:
Three weeks in, the guys have said yes to the call, they're thinking
about their purpose, and they're working on who they are in private. Now
comes the question underneath all of it: what is actually driving you?
Because you can follow Jesus in theory and still be completely
controlled by the pursuit of money, status, and success in practice.

This is one of the most relevant conversations you can have with a group
of guys in their mid-20s. You're all in the thick of building careers,
comparing yourselves to peers, and figuring out what 'making it' even
means. Jesus talks about money more than almost any other topic — not
because money is evil, but because it competes directly with God for the
throne of your life.

*"You can't serve two masters." That's not a suggestion. It's a
diagnosis.*

sections.heading: SCRIPTURE PASSAGES (ESV)
sections.body:
Matthew 6:19–24
19 *Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth
and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal,*
20 *but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither
moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal.*
21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
22 *The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy,
your whole body will be full of light,*
23 *but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of
darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the
darkness!*
24 *No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one
and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the
other. You cannot serve God and money.*
Matthew 6:33
33 *But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and
all these things will be added to you.*
Luke 12:15–21
15 *And he said to them, "Take care, and be on your guard against
all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of
his possessions."*
16 *And he told them a parable, saying, "The land of a rich man
produced plentifully,*
17 *and he thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have
nowhere to store my crops?'*
18 *And he said, 'I will do this: I will tear down my barns and
build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.*
19 *And I will say to my soul, "Soul, you have ample goods laid up
for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry."'*
20 *But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required
of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?'*
21 *So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich
toward God."*

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE to open. These are designed to surface the real motivations
guys carry without putting anyone on the defensive right away.

1.  What does 'making it' look like to you? Like if you hit it — what
    does that actually look like? *— disarming and gets guys to name
    what they're actually chasing*

2.  What's your honest relationship with money right now — stressed,
    chasing it, content, somewhere else? *— practical and relatable
    for guys in their 20s*

3.  Is there someone in your life — maybe someone you follow on social
    media — whose life you quietly want? What specifically about it?
    — gets at comparison and ambition without feeling churchy

4.  If your bank account and calendar showed someone else what you
    actually value — what would they conclude? *— convicting opener
    if the group is ready for it*

sections.heading: 2 — CONTEXT (5 MIN)
sections.body:
After reading through the passages together, share this background
before jumping into discussion:
Matthew 6:19–24

-   This is from the Sermon on the Mount — Jesus' most direct teaching
    on how to actually live.

-   "Treasures on earth" aren't just bank accounts — it's anything
    temporary you're building your security on.

-   The "eye" language in v.22–23 is about where your focus goes — if
    your gaze is fixed on wealth, your whole life orients toward it.

-   "You cannot serve both God and money" — the word 'serve' means to
    be enslaved to. Jesus is saying one of them owns you.
Luke 12:15–21 — The Rich Fool

-   A man's crops produce massively. His plan: build bigger barns, store
    everything, retire early. Sounds reasonable.

-   God calls him a fool — not because he was wealthy, but because he
    built his entire future on stuff that couldn't save him.

-   The man never asked what God wanted him to do with this. He only
    asked what he wanted.

-   Jesus ends: "This is how it will be with whoever stores up things
    for themselves but is not rich toward God."
*"The question isn't whether you have money or ambition. It's
whether money and ambition have you."*

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: WHAT YOU'RE CHASING (10 MIN)
sections.body:
These questions get at the real motivations underneath the surface. Pick
the ones that fit the room — you don't need all of them.

5.  When you imagine your life at 40, what does it look like? House,
    car, job, lifestyle. Where did that picture come from?

6.  Is there a number — a salary, a title, a milestone — that you've
    told yourself will finally make you feel okay? What happens when you
    hit it?

7.  Jesus says you're serving one master or the other. If you're being
    honest, which one is running more of your decisions right now?

8.  What do you spend most of your mental energy on during the day? Does
    that match what you say you value?

9.  How much does what other people have — or what they think of you
    — actually affect your decisions?

10. The rich fool's plan sounded reasonable. Are there any 'reasonable'
    plans in your life right now that don't actually include God?

11. Do you think there's a version of ambition and drive that's
    God-honoring? What does that look like vs. what you see around you?

12. What would you do differently with your time or money right now if
    you actually believed Jesus' promise in Matthew 6:33?

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: CONTENTMENT & ENOUGH (10 MIN)
sections.body:
The flip side of ambition is contentment — one of the hardest things
to actually have in your 20s. These questions go there.

13. Do you think contentment is something you have or something you
    practice? What's the difference?

14. Is there anything in your life right now that you have — that you
    once prayed for — that you've stopped being grateful for?

15. What does 'enough' actually look like for you? Have you ever defined
    it, or is it always just a little more than what you have?

16. Paul says he 'learned' contentment (Philippians 4:11) — it's not
    natural, it's trained. What do you think that training looks like
    day to day?

17. Is social media making contentment harder for you? Be honest about
    how it actually affects you.

18. What would it look like to be genuinely generous right now — at
    your current income, in your current situation? What's stopping you?

19. If the man in the parable had asked God what to do with the surplus
    instead of building bigger barns — what do you think God would
    have said?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
The rich fool wasn't condemned for working hard or being successful. He
was condemned for leaving God completely out of the equation — for
living as if the resources in his hands were his alone. The invitation
in Matthew 6:33 isn't to be poor or stop being ambitious. It's to
reorder what you're seeking first.
*"Seek first the kingdom — and all these things will be added. The
promise isn't poverty. It's priority."*

Leave the group with one of these to carry into the week:

20. What is one concrete way you could seek the kingdom first this week
    — with your time, your money, or your decisions?

21. Is there one area where you need to loosen your grip on something
    you've been holding too tightly?

22. What would it look like to bring God into one financial or career
    decision you've been making on your own?

Close in prayer — specifically over ambition, provision, and what it
means to trust God with the outcomes.
Leader tip: *Consider a 1-week challenge: each guy identifies one
thing he's been treating as a master instead of a tool — and picks
one practical step to reorder it. Report back next week.*

title: Who Are You When No One's Watching?
context:
Week 1 you looked at the call — saying yes to following Jesus like
Matthew did. Week 2 you dug into purpose and identity — the fact that
you were made for something specific. Week 3 is where it gets practical:
how do you actually live that out when life puts pressure on you?

Daniel is one of the most compelling figures in all of Scripture for
guys in their 20s. He's taken from everything familiar, dropped into a
culture that directly opposes his values, handed every reason to
compromise — and he doesn't. Not because he's perfect, but because
he'd already decided who he was before the pressure came.

*Integrity isn't what you do when people are watching. It's what
you've already decided to do before the moment arrives.*

sections.heading: WHY THIS PASSAGE
sections.body:

Daniel is one of the most compelling figures in all of Scripture for

*Integrity isn't what you do when people are watching. It's what
you've already decided to do before the moment arrives.*

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE of these to kick things off. Keep it light enough to warm up
the room but pointed enough to set the theme.

1.  Have you ever done the right thing when it would have been way
    easier to do the wrong thing? What happened? *— gets guys thinking
    about real moments, not theory*

2.  Is there a version of you that shows up at work or around certain
    people that's different from who you are here? What's different
    about him? — cuts right to the theme of private vs public self

3.  What's one area of your life where you feel like you're constantly
    fighting the same battle? *— honest and relatable, sets up the
    temptation angle*

4.  Who in your life do you respect most for how they actually live —
    not just what they believe? What makes them different? *— good if
    you want to start with inspiration before conviction*

sections.heading: 2 — SCRIPTURE & CONTEXT (8–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Read all three passages aloud. Go around the group — keep it moving,
don't stop to comment yet.

-   Daniel 1:1–8 — Daniel resolves not to defile himself

-   Daniel 6:1–10 — Daniel prays anyway, even when it's illegal

-   Proverbs 4:23 — Guard your heart, for everything flows from it

After reading, take 30 seconds of silence. Then give the group this
context:
Context on Daniel

-   Daniel was probably 14–17 years old when he was taken to Babylon. A
    teenager.

-   Babylon was the most powerful empire on earth — wealthy,
    seductive, and totally opposed to his faith.

-   He was given a new name, new food, new education — a full-scale
    identity replacement.

-   In chapter 1, his decision seems small: don't eat the king's food.
    But it was a line in the sand.

-   In chapter 6, he's now a powerful official — and he still kneels
    and prays, even when it could get him killed.

-   The key: Daniel didn't decide what he stood for in the moment of
    pressure. He'd already decided.
Context on Proverbs 4:23

-   "Heart" in Hebrew (lev) means the center of your will, thought, and
    emotion — not just feelings.

-   To "guard" it means to be intentional about what you let in and what
    you dwell on.

-   Everything you do flows from what's happening internally — your
    habits, your choices, your character.
*"Who you are in private is who you actually are. Everything else is
performance."*

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: THE PRIVATE LIFE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel's integrity wasn't built in the lion's den — it was built in
the small daily decisions that came before it. These questions go there.

5.  Is who you are in private consistent with who you are around other
    people? Where's the biggest gap?

6.  What do your habits look like when no one's holding you accountable
    — what you watch, how you spend your time, what you think about?

7.  Proverbs says everything flows from the heart. What are you
    currently letting into your heart that you know isn't helping you?

8.  Is there a line in the sand — something you've decided you won't
    do — or are most of your decisions made in the moment?

9.  When you're under pressure — stressed, tired, alone — who do you
    become? Is that who you want to be?

10. What would change if you lived every day like God actually sees
    everything? Not out of fear — but out of that being real to you?

11. Is there something you're doing privately right now that you'd be
    ashamed for the guys in this room to know about? *— hard question
    — only use if the group is ready for it*

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: PRESSURE & COMPROMISE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel faced real, external pressure to compromise — not just internal
temptation. These questions look at the moments where integrity actually
gets tested.

12. What's the biggest source of pressure in your life right now to be
    someone you're not?

13. Have you ever compromised on something you said you believed in
    because the cost felt too high? What happened?

14. Daniel made his decision before the pressure hit — he 'resolved'
    in chapter 1. Do you have any convictions like that? Things you've
    pre-decided?

15. Where in your life do you feel the most tempted to just go along
    with everyone else to avoid the friction?

16. Is there a situation in your life right now where you know what the
    right thing is but you haven't done it yet? What's holding you back?

17. What would it look like to be the Daniel in your friend group, your
    workplace, your family? What would have to change?

18. Do you think it's possible to maintain integrity in your 20s without
    a community around you holding you to it? Why or why not?

19. What's one area where you've been slowly drifting from who you want
    to be? When did it start?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Daniel didn't end up in the lion's den because he was reckless. He ended
up there because he was consistent. His integrity in the small things
built the character that held in the big moment. That's how it works for
all of us — character is built slowly, in private, long before
anyone's watching.
*"You don't rise to the level of your intentions. You fall to the
level of your habits."*

Leave the group with one of these to sit with this week:

20. What is one private habit or pattern you need to change this week
    — not for anyone else, but because of who you actually want to
    become?

21. Is there one area where you need to 'resolve' — pre-decide —
    before the moment of pressure comes?

22. What would the guy you want to be in 10 years tell the version of
    you right now to start doing differently?

Close in prayer. If the conversation got personal, pray specifically
over what came up — that makes it real and keeps the group connected
beyond the meeting.
Leader tip: *Consider ending with a 1-week challenge: each guy
picks one thing they're going to do differently in private this week
and shares it with the group. Check in on it next week. Accountability
is where this theme gets legs.*

sections.heading: 1 — OPEN UP (5 MIN)
sections.body:
Pick ONE of these to open — you don't need all of them. Just get guys
talking.

1.  If you could wake up tomorrow doing anything with your life — and
    money wasn't a factor — what would it be? Why don't you think
    that's realistic?

2.  What did you think you'd be doing with your life at 10 years old?
    How's that working out? —

3.  Is there something you feel like you were made to do but haven't
    done yet? What's stopping you?

4.  When someone asks what you do, do you actually feel like that's who
    you are? Or does it feel off?

sections.heading: 2 — SCRIPTURE & CONTEXT (8–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Go around and read both passages aloud. Keep it moving — don't comment
yet, just read.

-   Jeremiah 1:4–10

-   Ephesians 2:10

After reading, give 30–60 seconds of silence. Then share this context
before jumping into discussion:
Context on Jeremiah

-   He was young — likely a teenager or early 20s when God called him.

-   He was from a small town. Nobody. Not a religious celebrity.

-   His immediate response: "I don't know how to speak. I'm too young."

-   God's response: "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before
    you were born, I set you apart."

-   Jeremiah didn't feel ready. God said he already was.
Context on Ephesians 2:10

-   "Poiema" — the Greek word translated "workmanship" — is where we
    get the word "poem."

-   You are not an accident. You are something God crafted with
    intention.

-   The "good works" were prepared in advance — meaning purpose isn't
    something you create. It's something you walk into.
*"God's calling on your life isn't based on how ready you feel —
it's based on who He says you are."*

sections.heading: 3 — DISCUSSION: THE EXCUSES (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Jeremiah's first move when God called him was to explain why he couldn't
do it. Most of us do the same thing. Use any of these — you don't need
all of them. Follow the energy in the room.

5.  What's your version of "I'm too young / I don't know how"? What do
    you tell yourself disqualifies you?

6.  Is there something you've felt nudged toward — in faith, career,
    or relationships — that you've been putting off? What's the real
    reason?

7.  Do you actually believe God has a specific purpose for your life —
    or does that feel like something that applies to other people?

8.  Have you ever talked yourself out of something before even trying?
    What did you tell yourself?

9.  What's the difference between being genuinely not ready and just
    being scared?

10. If a close friend described what they think you're made for, what do
    you think they'd say? Does that match how you see yourself?

11. Is there an area of your life where you're waiting for permission to
    step into something — and who are you waiting for it from?

sections.heading: 4 — DISCUSSION: CREATED ON PURPOSE (10 MIN)
sections.body:
Flip it from the excuses to the truth. You are God's "poiema" — His
masterpiece. That's not a feel-good slogan; it's a theological statement
about how you were made and why. Pick the questions that fit your group.

12. What's one thing you're genuinely good at that you've maybe never
    thought of as something God gave you on purpose?

13. Are you currently living in a way that's moving toward your purpose
    — or are you mostly just filling time? Be honest.

14. What would change in your day-to-day life if you actually believed
    you were made for something specific?

15. What's the difference between your job and your calling? Do you
    think they have to be the same thing?

16. If God prepared good works for you "in advance," what do you think
    that means practically? Does it change how you make decisions?

17. Is there something you keep coming back to — a problem you want to
    solve, a type of person you want to help, something that makes you
    feel alive — that you've been dismissing as just a feeling?

18. Do you think God's purpose for your life is one big thing, or a lot
    of small faithful things? How does that change the pressure you put
    on yourself?

19. What would it look like to steward what you're already good at more
    intentionally this week?

sections.heading: 5 — CLOSE (5–10 MIN)
sections.body:
Don't end on a heavy question — land the plane with hope. Bring it
back to Jeremiah: he was scared, unqualified, and unsure. But he went.
And he became one of the most important voices in all of Scripture.
*"The question isn't whether God has a purpose for you. He does. The
question is whether you'll stop waiting to feel ready and start
walking in it."*

Leave the group with one of these closing questions to sit with — they
don't have to answer out loud:

20. What is one step — even a small one — you could take this week
    toward what you were made for?

21. Is there something God has been saying to you that you've been
    ignoring? What would it look like to stop ignoring it?

22. What would you do differently this week if you genuinely believed
    you were God's workmanship, created with intention?

Close in prayer. Keep it short and specific to what actually came up in
the room.
